The United Kingdom is a political union comprising England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. It is frequently confused with Great Britain, which is the geographical island containing England, Scotland, and Wales, and the British Isles, which is a geographical term including Ireland, the UK, and smaller islands. These distinctions lead to persistent errors in geography and international relations.

The United Kingdom as a political entity was formally established in 1707 when the Kingdom of Scotland merged with the Kingdom of England and Wales. Ireland joined in 1801, and the union became the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Great Britain is a geographical island containing England, Scotland, and Wales. But it does not include Northern Ireland, which is on the island of Ireland, and it does not include the Republic of Ireland either.

The British Isles is a purely geographical term encompassing the islands of Great Britain, Ireland, and thousands of smaller islands. This includes the Republic of Ireland, which is not part of the United Kingdom politically. The Republic of Ireland gained independence in 1922 and formally declared itself a republic in 1949. It is a sovereign nation not part of the UK, though it shares the island of Ireland with Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom but occupies the north of the island of Ireland. The island itself is divided between the UK, which includes Northern Ireland, and the Republic of Ireland, which is independent.

A common mistake is calling all of the British Isles "Britain" or "Great Britain," or calling the United Kingdom the "British Isles." Remember that the British Isles is purely geographical, not political.
